passages.text: Binary search operates on a sorted array using the half-open interval [lo, hi) where lo is included and hi is excluded. Initialize lo to 0 and hi to the array length.

sources.quote: Binary search requires a sorted array. Use the half-open interval [lo, hi): lo is included and hi is excluded. Initialize lo to zero and hi to the array length.

passages.text: The binary search algorithm iteratively narrows the search interval by comparing the target value with the middle element of the current interval. The loop continues while lo < hi. Compute mid = lo + floor((hi - lo) / 2). If array[mid] equals the target, return mid. If array[mid] is less than the target, set lo = mid + 1. Otherwise, set hi = mid. If the loop terminates without finding the target, return -1.

sources.quote: While lo is less than hi, set mid to lo plus floor((hi - lo) / 2). If array[mid] equals the target, return mid. If array[mid] is smaller, set lo to mid + 1. Otherwise set hi to mid. If the loop ends without a match, return -1.

passages.text: Example: Find the index of 12 in the sorted array [2, 5, 8, 12, 16]. Starting with lo = 0 and hi = 5, the first mid = 2 gives 8 (less than 12), so lo becomes 3. Next mid = 4 gives 16 (greater than 12), so hi becomes 4. The final mid = 3 gives 12, so return index 3.

sources.quote: Find 12 in [2, 5, 8, 12, 16]. With lo = 0 and hi = 5, mid = 2 gives 8, so lo becomes 3. Next mid = 4 gives 16, so hi becomes 4. Next mid = 3 gives 12. Return index 3.

passages.text: With constant-time array indexing, the worst-case time complexity of binary search is O(log n) because each iteration halves the search interval. This iterative implementation uses O(1) auxiliary space, and sorting costs are not included in this runtime analysis.

sources.quote: With constant-time array indexing, worst-case search time is O(log n), because each iteration roughly halves the interval. This iterative version uses O(1) auxiliary space. Sorting cost is excluded from that search-only runtime.

passages.text: Binary search allows duplicate values but does not guarantee finding the first occurrence. For exam purposes, students should track whether hi is included or excluded in the interval to avoid confusion.

sources.quote: Duplicates are allowed, but this version does not promise the first occurrence. For the exam, keep track of whether hi is included or excluded.

passages.text: Dijkstra's algorithm requires nonnegative edge weights, with zero-weight edges permitted but negative edge weights not allowed.

sources.quote: Correction: I misspoke. The standard Dijkstra algorithm requires nonnegative edge weights. Zero-weight edges are allowed. Do not write that negative edges are supported.

passages.text: The relaxation step for an edge (u, v) involves comparing the current distance to v with the candidate distance dist[u] + weight(u, v). If the candidate distance is smaller, update dist[v] to this candidate and set predecessor[v] to u.

sources.quote: Relaxing an edge (u, v) means checking whether dist[u] + weight(u, v) is smaller than dist[v]. If it is, update dist[v] to that candidate distance and set predecessor[v] to u.

blocks.topic: Separating trusted instructions from untrusted material

passages.text: When processing tool results, it is critical to distinguish between trusted instructions (which are explicitly provided by the user) and untrusted retrieved material (which may contain adversarial text). Reading untrusted material does not grant authorization to execute the requested actions within the system.

sources.quote: Separate trusted instructions from untrusted retrieved material. A tool result can contain adversarial text; reading it does not authorize its requested actions.
